classification.difficultyReason: Combine circle geometry, a trigonometric area model, differentiation and a geometric proof of the maximising triangle.

content.prompt: An isosceles triangle $PQR$ is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$ of radius 1 unit, as shown in the diagram. Let $\angle QOR=2\theta$, where $\theta$ is acute.

spec.description: Unshaded circle with an inscribed isosceles triangle, matching single ticks on PQ and PR, dashed radii OQ and OR, and the central angle labelled 2θ. The construction through P and O and point M are absent.
spec.mathematics: OP=OQ=OR=1; PQ=PR; P lies on the perpendicular bisector of chord QR; angle QOR=2θ. Coordinates provide a schematic view and supply no numerical angle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; M and the requested construction are reserved for the response.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Join $PO$ and extend it to meet $QR$ at $M$. Then prove that $QM=\sin\theta$ and $OM=\cos\theta$.

answer.short: $QM=\sin\theta$ and $OM=\cos\theta$, using right triangle $OQM$ with hypotenuse $OQ=1$.
answer.worked:
Since $PQ=PR$ and $OQ=OR$, both $P$ and $O$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $QR$. Thus the line $PO$ meets $QR$ at its midpoint $M$ and $OM\perp QR$. The congruent right triangles $OQM$ and $ORM$ give $\angle QOM=\theta$.

$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{QM}{OQ}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{QM}{1}\\\sin\theta&=QM,\\\cos\theta&=\frac{OM}{OQ}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{OM}{1}\\\cos\theta&=OM.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Complete solution figure adds PM through O, the midpoint M, a derived right-angle mark and the two equal central half-angles.
spec.mathematics: M is the midpoint of QR, PM is perpendicular to QR, and angle QOM=angle MOR=θ.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution-only construction and derived angle labels.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the area $A$ of $\triangle PQR$ is $A=\sin\theta(\cos\theta+1)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence show that, as $\theta$ varies, $\triangle PQR$ has its maximum possible area when it is equilateral.

answer.short: The maximum occurs at $\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$. Then $\angle QOR=\angle POQ=\angle POR=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, so the equal chords $PQ$, $PR$ and $QR$ form an equilateral triangle.
answer.worked:
For $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$,

$$\begin{align*}A&=\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)\\A&=\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta\\A&=\sin\theta+\frac12\sin2\theta,\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=\cos\theta+\cos2\theta\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=\cos\theta+2\cos^2\theta-1\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1).\end{align*}$$

At a stationary point,

$$\begin{align*}(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$

Thus $2\cos\theta-1=0$ or $\cos\theta+1=0$. Since $\theta$ is acute, $\cos\theta>0$, so $\cos\theta=-1$ is excluded.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos\theta-1&=0\\2\cos\theta&=1\\\cos\theta&=\frac12\\\theta&=\frac{\pi}{3}.\end{align*}$$

Check the maximum:

$$\begin{align*}\frac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=-\sin\theta-2\sin2\theta\\\left.\frac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}\right|_{\theta=\pi/3}&=-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}<0.\end{align*}$$

This stationary point is a maximum. Moreover, $\cos\theta+1>0$, so $\frac{dA}{d\theta}>0$ before $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{dA}{d\theta}<0$ after it throughout the acute domain. Hence it is the global maximum.

Triangles $POQ$ and $POR$ are congruent by SSS: $PO$ is common, $OQ=OR$ and $PQ=PR$. Therefore $\angle POQ=\angle POR$. At the maximum,

$$\begin{align*}\angle QOR&=2\theta\\\angle QOR&=\frac{2\pi}{3},\\\angle POQ=\angle POR&=\frac12(2\pi-\angle QOR)\\\angle POQ=\angle POR&=\frac12\left(2\pi-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\\\angle POQ=\angle POR&=\frac{2\pi}{3}.\end{align*}$$

The vertices are evenly spaced around the circle. Equal central angles subtend equal chords, so $PQ=PR=QR$ and the triangle is equilateral.
